title: Body folding

objective.text: Explain how folding turns the flat embryonic disc into a curled body.

body.general: How does a flat sheet become a curled body? The brain and neural tube (future spinal cord) grow fast and lengthen [f1]. This makes the flat disc bulge into the fluid sac above it, the amniotic cavity [f1]. Head and tail then swing underneath, curling the embryo up [f2]. Meanwhile the two sides fold down and meet in front, closing the front body wall [f4]. It stays open only at the future navel [f5]. Folding tucks part of the yolk sac inside as gut; the rest stays outside on a stalk, the vitelline duct [f7].
body.mbbs: Rapid growth of the brain and lengthening of the neural tube make the flat disc bulge into the amniotic cavity [f1]. Head and tail folds swing ventrally, and the embryo curls into the fetal position [f2]. Folding is under way by days 24–25, and the body is tightly C-shaped by days 31–35 [f3]. At the same time two lateral body-wall folds move ventrally and close the ventral body wall [f4]. The wall stays open only at the umbilical region, where the connecting stalk and yolk-sac duct attach [f5]. The folds draw the amnion around the embryo, which ends up inside the amniotic cavity [f6]. Folding takes part of the yolk sac in as gut; the rest stays outside, linked by the vitelline duct [f7].

facts.text: Growth of the brain and lengthening of the neural tube make the flat disc bulge into the amniotic cavity.
Head and tail folds swing ventrally and the embryo curls into the fetal position.
Folding is under way by days 24–25, and the body is tightly C-shaped by days 31–35.
At the same time two lateral body-wall folds move ventrally and close the ventral body wall.
The ventral body wall stays open only at the umbilical region, where the connecting stalk and yolk-sac duct attach.
The folds pull the amnion around the embryo, so the embryo ends up inside the amniotic cavity.
Folding takes in only part of the yolk sac as gut; the rest stays outside, linked by the vitelline duct.
Failure of the lateral folds to close gives ventral body-wall defects.

misconceptions.wrong: The whole yolk sac becomes the gut.
misconceptions.right: Only the part taken in by folding becomes gut; the rest stays outside, linked by the vitelline duct.

checks.prompt: What mainly drives the head and tail folds?
options: Fast growth of the brain and neural tube
checks.why: The growing brain and lengthening neural tube make the disc bulge and its ends swing ventrally.

checks.prompt: After the side folds close, where does the belly wall stay open?
checks.why: The connecting stalk still attaches at the umbilical region, so the wall stays open there.

checks.prompt: What happens to the yolk sac during folding?
options: All of it becomes the gut
Only part of it becomes gut
checks.why: Only the part taken in becomes gut; the rest stays outside, joined to the gut by the vitelline duct.

adult: The closed side folds become the front wall of the chest and belly, with the navel as the last opening [f4,f5].
clinical: If the two side folds do not close, the baby has a gap in the front body wall [f8]. These are called ventral body-wall defects [f8].

remember.q: What makes the flat disc fold?
remember.a: Growth of the brain and neural tube, which bulge it into the amniotic cavity [f1].

remember.q: Where does the belly wall stay open after folding?
remember.a: At the umbilical region, where the connecting stalk and yolk-sac duct attach [f5].

remember.q: Does the whole yolk sac become gut?
remember.a: No: only the part taken in; the rest stays outside on the vitelline duct [f7].
